“Dr. Waldron, Elsie needs help!” Elsie’s husband was adamant, almost angry, as he stared at me. On the other hand, Elsie stared at the floor, almost as though she wasn’t present. I had never met either of the couple before and was struggling just a little to figure out what was needed from me to help her.

“What is going on?” I asked as I flipped through her chart. This was still in the days of paper charts, and I headed to the lab section of her chart. There wasn’t anything too crazy that I could see there—her liver enzymes were a little elevated, but otherwise, everything seemed OK.

“It’s her drinking!” Her husband told me. “She is drinking more and more every night. She won’t go out except to get whiskey. She drinks till she passes out every night and has to have something every morning to get her started.”

“Is that true?” I asked Elsie, feeling like a judge overseeing a jury trial.

“Yes,” she said. Her face was emotionless, and I couldn’t tell if she wanted to be there or not.

“Do you want help?” I asked her. This was a loaded question. Many people who struggle with alcoholism aren’t ready to break free from its vice-like hold on them. Maybe Elsie was different.

“I guess so,” she said, indifferently. Once again, I couldn’t tell whether she wanted to be there or not.

“At the rate at which you are drinking, you will kill yourself within a year – maybe two at best – if you don’t give up alcohol entirely,” I told her. “If you want to, I will try to find you an inpatient program to detox you and get you off of alcohol.”

“She’s ready,” he husband said firmly.

When dealing with someone who drinks heavily, it is crucial that they don’t simply stop drinking without medical support. Abrupt cessation of alcohol use causes the body to go into withdrawal which can produce a state called Delirium Tremens and even seizures.

I stepped out of the exam room and to make phone calls. It is never easy to find a place for someone to attempt to rehabilitate from any kind of substances, and it was over an hour and a half before I found a facility that was willing to take Elsie and try to help her get off of the whiskey.

I sighed as I reentered her exam room. I had been afraid that I wouldn’t find anywhere for her to go.

I told them about the plan, and her husband nodded vigorously, while Elise continued to stare silently at the floor. “Can we pray together before you go?” I asked them, and when they nodded assent, I prayed with them, asking for freedom and Jesus’ presence in both of their lives.

They left my office with marching orders and directions on where to go. I had a happy glow about me for the rest of the morning, knowing that I had gone the extra mile and had really made a difference in this middle-aged couple’s life.

Around 2 pm, I got a call from the rehab facility. They hadn’t seen even a shadow of Elsie or her husband, which was surprising, since it was a bright sunny day and the facility wasn’t that far away. With a sinking feeling, I dialed the couple’s phone number.

“She won’t go!” Her husband told me. “She tells me that she told me this ahead of time. She’ll try to cut back, but she isn’t willing to go into a rehab facility or any such thing. I guess just tell them that we’ll let them know if she changes her mind.”

My nurse called the rehab facility and told them the bad news, and I sat down in my chair, stunned. What else could I have done? Was there a solution for Elsie—something different that I could have said that would have made a difference in her life?

About a year later, I received the sad news that Elsie had died at home. I was certain that things would have been different if she had gone to rehab and if she had given control to Jesus. None of that had happened, and I felt cynicism pushing into my heart.

Cynicism

We live in an age of cynicism. In ancient Greece, the cynics were an odd assortment of men who specialized in being grouchy and saying mean (they would have said truthful) things to people. They often dressed in rags and behaved in such a way that most of the polite Athenians did not want to be close to them.

Today, cynicism means a tendency to believe the worst about people and circumstances. Cynical people believe that all people are motivated purely by selfishness and that bad events will tend to prevail.

Many young doctors are idealistic and very hopeful. They believe that if they exert the utmost effort, they can make a real, positive impact on their patient’s lives. Unfortunately, as time goes by and they try their hardest and their patients don’t change, they can give up. These doctors still try, but they no longer really hope that their efforts will make much of a difference.

It seems as though people who get involved with politics often have the best of intentions. They see this as a path to changing society for the better. Unfortunately, as time goes by and the faces in charge change, the policies don’t really change, they tend to become cynical.

Sometimes this cynicism is directed against all politicians. Sometimes it is only anger directed against members of the party that opposes their party’s positions. Hope is replaced by cynicism.

Cynicism in the Bible

If there is a book in the Bible that seems to have been written by a cynical man, it is the book of Ecclesiastes. The Preacher, who we understand to be Solomon, lists all of the things that he endeavored in an attempt to find joy.

In chapter 2:17-23 Solomon describes work as futile. He finishes by saying, “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

He saw the world as being dominated by tyrants and there was little that the people could do about it. Solomon went so far as to say that political power was meaningless “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Ecclesiastes 6:6, he seems to disparage long life. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Of course, he finishes his short book with the instruction to remember our Creator in the days of our youth. There is a blessing for those who choose to focus on God when they have a little bit of energy left and not, when they are old and jaded, like Solomon.

Later on, it almost seemed as though God had given up on His people. He still sent prophets to them, but He knew without a doubt that the people would refuse to respond. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Even in the New Testament, Paul told Timothy that the time was coming when people would no longer listen to sound doctrine. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

By picking and choosing these passages, we can come away with a very gloomy view of the future and, more specifically, of human’s willingness to change. It seems there is little point of investing ourselves in the people around us. They are full of woe and are as likely to change as a chipmunk is to master differential calculus.

The Opposite of Cynicism

The opposite of cynicism is hope. It is the belief that the future could be better.

It is interesting that the Apostle Paul spoke of tribulations in the Epistle to the Romans, “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

We may not have reached the place where we glory in the trials we experience, but certainly, they should bring us these other things that he mentions. For, we grow in patience and experience, even as we deal with trials, but more than that, we come to realize that we have hope for tomorrow because we serve a great God.

The contrast in the story of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15 teaches us much about hope. The father and the older brother were strikingly different in their attitudes.

The father had never given up hope – he knew that his son had failed him and gone far from what he knew was right and yet, the father still desired to see the prodigal come to himself and return home.

On the other hand, the older brother not only had no hope for his younger brother, but he was also angry with him. The prodigal had wasted his money, he had lived in sin, and now, he had returned home just because he was out of money.

Certainly, there was no reason to trust the younger son. Yet, that is exactly what our Heavenly Father does for us.

Look for Hope in the Right Places

Part of the problem is that we look for hope in the wrong places. A number of years ago, a presidential candidate ran for office under the slogan “Hope and Change,” and yet, even though he was elected, I imagine most folks did not feel that their lives were significantly changed for the better.

Pursuing the things this world values—political power and wealth is guaranteed to bring emptiness. This is Satan’s pattern—he always over-promises and under-delivers.

This was what he did when he tempted Jesus, “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). All of the things Satan offered, nothing compared with the glory that Jesus eventually received from the road that led to the cross.

In the same way, Satan would like to distract Christians from seeking the things that are valuable, and that will bring hope. Satan tells Christians that politics will not only change the world for the better, it is an easier way to change the world.

The Bible is clear that we build hope as we nurture our relationship with God and then work to help our brothers and sisters build that same relationship in their own lives. The reason that we can hope is not because people are so wonderful—we don’t have to live very long to realize that they aren’t. The reason we hope is because we serve an awesome, faithful God who walks with us through the worst of our trials.

Remember that We Have Undeserved Hope

Jesus’ messages about forgiveness make it clear that one of the major reasons that we have for forgiving others in our lives is that we have received great and undeserved forgiveness. The same is true for hope.

Each one of us was hopeless and without reason to expect to receive hope and we were still given a ray of light in the midst of our darkness. Maybe part of the reason that we have so much trouble hoping for good things for the people around us is that we do not remember how hopeless we were before we found grace.

If Jesus was able to bring hope to our hopeless existence, then certainly He can do wonderful things in the hearts and lives of others around us. The only people we should give up on are the ones that our Savior has given up on as well.

Small Efforts Do Make a Difference

I remember having a conversation with a young person who was planning to go into medicine and had a plan to go to a foreign country and serve the people there. As we were talking, an older man entered the conversation and shared that he saw little hope for change in developing countries.

The people in those countries just weren’t interested in getting better and didn’t do the minimum necessary to stave off things like worms and parasites. Doctors and nurses couldn’t make a difference in such an environment.

I could sense the heart of the youth sinking as this older man shared. He had experience, and he had given up hope. The sad thing was that he was also stealing the hope of someone who still had a desire to serve.

When I was in training, I had a surgeon tell me that family doctors didn’t really do anything. They simply kept their patients alive till their next office visit, whereas surgeons really “fixed” people—taking out (or off) the offending body part.

At the end of the day, small efforts do make a difference. I don’t do brain surgery, but I still can make a difference in someone else’s life— maybe just by spending a little time and listening and praying. This is true for all of us.

More than that, we come to realize that making this effort changes our own lives for the better. Jesus told the sheep that as they ministered to “the least of these my brethren,” they were ministering to Him.

Even if no one’s life is improved, our Savior knows our desires and feels our efforts, and will reward them someday.

A Few Things to Remember

When we face failures, we tend to move in one of two directions. Those of us who are optimists tend to believe that this episode was an isolated event and that the future is still bright. On the other hand, pessimists believe that failures are permanent, personal, and pervasive.

Pessimists believe that their failures are the result of intrinsic character flaws that they have and that these things affect all of their lives and are unlikely to change. Unlike the righteous man who falls to rise again, these people fall and lie where they fall, defeated at the outset.

When we are dealing with other people, we need to give them the same grace that we should give ourselves. They, too, are growing, and if they have a failure today, they will do better tomorrow. Maybe they will fail again, but they will at least “fail better.”

Conclusion

Cynicism is rife in our world. Many have given up hope for a better future, and it is understandable for those who have invested their hope in this world’s institutions. There is no real hope in government or in armies or in bureaucracy.

The song says, “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” For, Jesus is the one who brings light into our darkness and allows us to continue, even when others fail us.

God is the one who redeems us. He is the one who sent the prophets, even though their messages were ignored, and the prophets were persecuted. He is the one who continues to hope for us, even when we have failed Him so many times in the past.

He is the reason we carry on. He is the reason that we have hope, not only for ourselves but also for our brothers.

“Dr. Waldron, Elsie het hulp nodig!” Elsie se man was vasbeslote, amper kwaad, terwyl hy na my staar. Aan die ander kant het Elsie na die vloer gestaar, amper asof sy nie teenwoordig was nie. Ek het nog nooit die paartjie tevore ontmoet nie en het ’n bietjie gesukkel om te verstaan wat van my verwag is om haar te help.

“Wat gebeur?” het ek gevra terwyl ek deur haar dossier blaai. Dit was nog in die dae van papierdossiers, en ek het na die laboratoriumafdeling van haar dossier gegaan. Daar was niks te buitengewoon wat ek daar kon sien nie—haar lewerensieme was effens verhoog, maar andersins het alles okay gelyk.

“Dis haar drink!” haar man het vir my gesê. “Sy drink elke aand meer en meer. Sy gaan nie uit nie behalwe om whiskey te kry. Sy drink tot sy flouval elke aand en moet elke oggend iets hê om haar aan die gang te kry.”

“Is dit waar?” het ek vir Elsie gevra, en ek het gevoel soos ’n regter wat ’n jurielei toesig hou.

“Ja,” het sy gesê. Haar gesig was uitdrukkingsloos, en ek kon nie sê of sy daar wou wees nie.

“Wil jy hulp hê?” het ek haar gevra. Dit was ’n gelaaide vraag. Baie mense wat met alkoholisme sukkel, is nie gereed om van die greep daarvan ontslae te raak nie. Miskien was Elsie anders.

“Ek dink so,” het sy onverskillig gesê. Weer kon ek nie seker wees of sy daar wou wees of nie.

“Teen die tempo waarop jy drink, sal jy jouself binne ’n jaar—miskien twee op die beste—vermoor as jy nie heeltemal met alkohol ophou nie,” het ek vir haar gesê. “As jy wil, sal ek probeer om ’n intramurale program vir jou te kry om jou te detoksifiseer en van alkohol af te kry.”

“Sy is gereed,” het die man vas gesê.

Wanneer jy met iemand te make het wat swaar drink, is dit noodsaaklik dat hulle nie net ophou drink sonder mediese ondersteuning nie. Skielike staking van alkoholgebruik veroorsaak dat die liggaam onttrekking ervaar wat ’n toestand kan veroorsaak wat Delirium Tremens genoem word en selfs toevalle kan gee.

Ek het uit die ondersoekkamer gestap om oproepe te maak. Dit is nooit maklik om ’n plek te kry waar iemand kan probeer rehabiliteer van enige soort dwelmmisbruik nie, en dit het meer as ’n uur en ’n half geneem voordat ek ’n fasiliteit gevind het wat bereid was om Elsie te neem en te probeer help om van die whiskey af te kom.

Ek het gesug toe ek die ondersoekkamer weer binnekom. Ek was bang dat ek geen plek sou kry wat haar kon help nie.

Ek het hulle van die plan vertel, en haar man het hewig geknik, terwyl Elsie steeds stilletjies na die vloer gestaar het. “Kan ons saam bid voordat jy gaan?” het ek hulle gevra, en toe hulle instem, het ek saam met hulle gebid en gevra vir vryheid en Jesus se teenwoordigheid in albei se lewens.

Hulle het my kantoor verlaat met instruksies en aanwysings waarheen om te gaan. Ek het die res van die oggend ’n gelukkige gloed gevoel, wetende dat ek die ekstra myl geloop het en regtig ’n verskil in die middeljarige paartjie se lewe gemaak het.

Omstreeks 14:00 het ek ’n oproep van die rehabilitasiefasiliteit ontvang. Hulle het nie eens ’n skadu van Elsie of haar man gesien nie, wat verrassend was aangesien dit ’n helder sonnige dag was en die fasiliteit nie ver weg was nie. Met ’n sinkende gevoel het ek die paartjie se telefoonnommer gedraai.

“Sy sal nie gaan nie!” het haar man vir my gesê. “Sy sê sy het my dit vooruit vertel. Sy sal probeer om minder te drink, maar sy is nie bereid om in ’n rehabilitasiefasiliteit of iets dergeliks te gaan nie. Ek dink vertel net vir hulle dat ons hulle sal laat weet as sy van plan verander.”

My verpleegster het die rehabilitasiefasiliteit gebel en vir hulle die slegte nuus vertel, en ek het in my stoel gaan sit, verstom. Wat anders kon ek nog gedoen het? Was daar ’n oplossing vir Elsie—iets anders wat ek kon gesê het wat ’n verskil in haar lewe sou maak?

Ongeveer ’n jaar later het ek die hartseer nuus ontvang dat Elsie by die huis oorlede is. Ek was oortuig dat dinge anders sou gewees het as sy na rehabilitasie gegaan het en as sy beheer aan Jesus oorhandig het. Niks van dit het gebeur nie, en ek het gevoel hoe cinisme in my hart begin insluip.

Kynisme

Ons lewe in ’n tyd van kynisme. In die antieke Griekeland was die kynici ’n vreemde groep mans wat daarop gespesialiseer het om morsig te wees en gemene (hulle sou gesê het ware) dinge vir mense te sê. Hulle het dikwels in lompe aangetrek en op ’n wyse gedra wat die meeste van die netjiese Athens nie naby hulle wou wees nie.

Vandag beteken kynisme ’n neiging om die slegste oor mense en omstandighede te glo. Kyniese mense glo dat alle mense suiwer deur selfbelang gemotiveer is en dat slegte gebeure geneig is om te oorheers.

Baie jong dokters is idealisties en baie hoopvol. Hulle glo dat as hulle uiterste poging aanwend, hulle ’n werklike, positiewe impak op hul pasiënte se lewens kan hê. Ongelukkig, namate tyd verloop en hulle hul bes probeer en hul pasiënte nie verander nie, kan hulle opgee. Hierdie dokters probeer steeds, maar hulle hoop nie meer regtig dat hul pogings veel van ’n verskil sal maak nie.

Dit lyk asof mense wat betrokke raak by politiek dikwels die beste bedoelings het. Hulle sien dit as ’n pad om die samelewing tot die beter te verander. Ongelukkig, namate tyd verloop en die gesigte aan bewind verander, maar die beleidsrigtings nie regtig verander nie, neig hulle om kynies te raak.

Somtyds is hierdie kynisme teen alle politikus gerig. Soms is dit net woede teen lede van die party wat die teenoorgestelde standpunte van hul eie party inneem. Hoop word vervang deur kynisme.

Kynisme in die Bybel

As daar ’n boek in die Bybel is wat lyk of dit deur ’n kyniese man geskryf is, is dit Prediker. Die Prediker, wat ons verstaan as Salomo, noem al die dinge waarin hy hom beproef het in ’n poging om vreugde te vind.

In hoofstuk 2:17-23 beskryf Salomo werk as nutteloos. Hy eindig deur te sê, “For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.” (Ecclesiastes 2:22,23)

Hy het die wêreld as deur tiranne oorheers beskou en daar was min wat die mense daaraan kon doen. Salomo het so ver gegaan om te sê dat politieke mag sinloos was: “Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished. For out of prison he cometh to reign; whereas also he that is born in his kingdom becometh poor” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

In Prediker 6:6 lyk dit asof hy lang lewe minag. “Yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place?”

Natuurlik eindig hy sy kort boek met die instruksie om ons Skepper te onthou in die dae van ons jeug. Daar is ’n seën vir diegene wat kies om op God te fokus wanneer hulle nog ’n bietjie energie oor het en nie wanneer hulle oud en afgeveel is soos Salomo nie.

Later het dit amper gelyk asof God sy rug op Sy volk gedraai het. Hy het steeds profete gestuur, maar Hy het sonder twyfel geweet dat die volk sou weier om te reageer. “Therefore thou shalt speak all these words unto them; but they will not hearken to thee: thou shalt also call unto them; but they will not answer thee” (Jeremiah 7:27).

Selfs in die Nuwe Testament het Paulus vir Timoteus gesê dat ’n tyd sou kom wanneer mense nie meer na gesonde leer sou luister nie. “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;” (2 Timothy 4:3).

Deur hierdie gedeeltes uit te kies en te kies, kan ons met ’n baie somber siening van die toekoms en, meer spesifiek, van mense se bereidheid om te verander wegkom. Dit lyk asof dit min sin het om onsself in die mense om ons te belê. Hulle is vol ellende en is so geneig om te verander soos ’n grondeekhorinkie geneig sou wees om differensiaalrekening te bemeester.

Die Teenoorgestelde van Kynisme

Die teenoorgestelde van kynisme is hoop. Dit is die geloof dat die toekoms beter kan wees.

Dit is interessant dat die apostel Paulus van verdrukking praat in die Brief aan die Romeine: “And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:3-5).

Ons mag nog nie die plek bereik waar ons in die beproewinge wat ons ervaar verheug nie, maar sekerlik behoort hulle ons die ander dinge wat hy noem te bring. Want ons groei in geduld en ondervinding, selfs terwyl ons beproewinge deurmaak, maar meer as dit, besef ons dat ons hoop het vir môre omdat ons ’n groot God dien.

Die kontras in die verhaal van die Verloren Seun in Lukas 15 leer ons baie oor hoop. Die vader en die ouer broer was opvallend verskillend in hul houdings.

Die vader het nooit die hoop opgegee nie—hy het geweet dat sy seun hom teleurgestel en ver van regte weggedwaal het en tog het die vader steeds begeer om die verlorene tot kennis van homself te laat kom en huis toe te laat terugkeer.

Aan die ander kant het die ouer broer nie net geen hoop vir sy jonger broer gehad nie, maar hy was ook kwaad vir hom. Die verlorene het sy geld verkwis, hy het in sonde geleef, en nou het hy huis toe gekom net omdat hy geen geld meer gehad het nie.

Daar was sekerlik geen rede om die jonger seun te vertrou nie. Tog is dit presies wat ons Hemelse Vader vir ons doen.

Soek Hoop Op Die Regte Plekke

’n Deel van die probleem is dat ons hoop op die verkeerde plekke soek. ’n Aantal jare gelede het ’n presidensiële kandidaat onder die leuse “Hope and Change” veldtog gevoer, en tog, selfs al is hy verkies, dink ek nie die meeste mense het gevoel dat hul lewens beduidend tot die beter verander is nie.

Om die dinge na te streef wat hierdie wêreld waardeer—politieke mag en rykdom—is ’n resep om leegheid te ervaar. Dit is die duiwel se patroon—hy bel oorslaan en lewer min.

Dit is wat hy gedoen het toe hy Jesus verlei het: “All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8). Al die dinge wat die Satan aangebied het, niks was vergelykbaar met die heerlikheid wat Jesus uiteindelik van die pad na die kruis ontvang het nie.

Op dieselfde manier sou die duiwel Christene daarvan wil aflei om die dinge te soek wat waardevol is en wat hoop bring. Satan vertel Christene dat politiek nie net die wêreld tot die beter sal verander nie, dit is ’n maklike manier om die wêreld te verander.

Die Bybel is duidelik dat ons hoop bou soos ons ons verhouding met God spertyd en dan werk om te help dat ons broers en susters daardie selfde verhouding in hul eie lewens bou. Die rede dat ons kan hoop is nie omdat mense so wonderlik is nie—ons hoef nie lank te lewe om te besef dat hulle nie is nie. Die rede dat ons hoop is omdat ons ’n ontzaglike, getroue God dien wat met ons deur die ergste van ons beproewinge wandel.

Onthou Dat Ons Onverdiende Hoop Het

Jesus se boodskappe oor vergifnis maak dit duidelik dat een van die hoofredes waarom ons ander in ons lewens moet vergewe, is dat ons groot en onverdiende vergifnis ontvang het. Dieselfde geld vir hoop.

Elkeen van ons was hopeloos en sonder rede om te verwag om hoop te ontvang en tog is ’n straal lig in die middel van ons duisternis aan ons gegee. Miskien is ’n deel van die rede waarom ons soveel moeite het om goed te hoop vir die mense rondom ons, dat ons nie onthou hoe hopeloos ons was voordat ons genade gevind het nie.

As Jesus in staat was om hoop in ons hopelose bestaan te bring, dan kan Hy sekerlik wonderlike dinge in die harte en lewens van ander rondom ons doen. Die enigste mense op wie ons moet opgee, is dié wat ons Verlosser ook opgegee het.

Klein Pogings Maak Wel ’n Verskil

Ek onthou ’n gesprek met ’n jong persoon wat beplan het om in die geneeskunde in te gaan en ’n plan gehad het om na ’n buiteland te gaan en daar die mense te dien. Terwyl ons gepraat het, het ’n ouer man by die gesprek aangesluit en gedeel dat hy min hoop vir verandering in ontwikkelende lande sien.

Die mense in daardie lande was net nie geïnteresseerd om beter te word nie en het nie die minimum gedoen wat nodig is om dinge soos wurms en parasiete te voorkom nie. Dokters en verpleegpersone kon nie ’n verskil maak in so ’n omgewing nie.

Ek kon die jeug se hart voel sink toe hierdie ouer man gepraat het. Hy het ervaring gehad, en hy het die hoop opgegee. Die hartseer ding was dat hy ook die hoop gesteel het van iemand wat nog die begeerte gehad het om te dien.

Toe ek in opleiding was, het ’n chirurg vir my gesê dat familieartsen regtig niks doen nie. Hulle hou net hul pasiënte lewendig tot hul volgende spreekkamerbesoek, terwyl chirurge regtig mense “vasmaak”—deur die aanstootlike liggaamsdeel te verwyder (of af te haal).

Aan die einde van die dag maak klein pogings wel ’n verskil. Ek doen nie breinkirurgie nie, maar ek kan steeds ’n verskil in iemand anders se lewe maak—miskien net deur ’n bietjie tyd te spandeer en te luister en te bid. Dit geld vir ons almal.

Meer as dit, besef ons dat om hierdie poging te doen ons eie lewens vir die beter verander. Jesus het vir die skape gesê dat toe hulle aan “die minste van hierdie my broeders” diens bewys het, hulle aan Hom diens bewys het.

Selfs as niemand se lewe verbeter nie, ken ons Verlosser ons begeertes en voel ons pogings, en sal hulle eendag beloon.

’n Paar Dinge Om Te Onthou

Wanneer ons teëspoed ervaar, neig ons om in een van twee rigtings te beweeg. Diegene van ons wat optimiste is, neig om te glo dat die episode ’n geïsoleerde voorval was en dat die toekoms steeds helder is. Aan die ander kant glo pessimiste dat mislukkings permanent, persoonlik en wydverspreid is.

Pessimiste glo dat hul mislukkings die gevolg is van intrinsieke karaktergebreke wat hulle het en dat hierdie dinge al hul lewens raak en onwaarskynlik sal verander. Anders as die regverdige man wat val om weer op te staan, val hierdie mense en bly lê waar hulle val, verslaan van die begin af.

Wanneer ons met ander mense werk, moet ons hulle dieselfde genade gee wat ons onsself behoort te gee. Hulle groei ook, en as hulle vandag ’n mislukking het, sal hulle môre beter doen. Miskien sal hulle weer misluk, maar hulle sal ten minste “beter misluk.”

Gevolgtrekking

Kynisme is volop in ons wêreld. Baie het die hoop op ’n beter toekoms opgegee, en dit is verstaanbaar vir dié wat hul hoop in hierdie wêreld se instellings belê het. Daar is geen werklike hoop in regering of in leërs of in burokrasie nie.

Die lied sê, “Oh to have no hope in Jesus, how dark this world must be!” Want Jesus is die een wat lig in ons duisternis bring en ons in staat stel om voort te gaan, selfs wanneer ander ons teleurstel.

God is die een wat ons red. Hy is die een wat die profete gestuur het, selfs al is hulle se boodskappe geïgnoreer en die profete vervolg. Hy is die een wat aanhou hoop vir ons, selfs wanneer ons Hom soveel kere in die verlede teleurgestel het.

Hy is die rede dat ons voortgaan. Hy is die rede dat ons hoop het, nie net vir onsself nie maar ook vir ons broers.

How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

As minister in the church, John continued to be more and more troubled by the slave trade that was still going on. In 1788, 34 years after he left the slave trade, He wrote a book entitled Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade and sent it to all the members of parliament. This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

The tune “Amazing Grace” is an early American folk melody. It was first known as a plantation melody entitled “Loving Lambs”. This tune was first published in 1831 in the book The Virginia Harmony. The majority of hymn books published after this time included this song. In 1910, Edwin O. Excell added the last verse, which eventually replaced the last three original verses of the song. His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Several other Olney hymns by Newton continue to be sung today, including “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” and “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

Hoe ongelooflik is dit dat God ’n ellendige sondaar, sonder die vrees van die Here, kan neem en hom in ’n deur die bloed gewas heilige en prediker van die evangelie kan verander! In hierdie verhaal sien ons God se lewe-veranderende krag werk in ons gesangskrywer se lewe.

In die klein kerkhof van ’n kerkhof in Olney, Engeland, staan ’n granietgrafsteen met hierdie inskripsie, deur Newton self geskryf voor sy dood:

John Newton, eens ’n ongelowige en losbol, ’n dienaar van slawe in Afrika, is, deur die ryk barmhartigheid van ons Here en Verlosser Jesus Christus, bewaar, herstel, vergewe, en aangestel om die geloof te preek wat hy lank daaraan gewerk het om te vernietig!

Hierdie epitaaf beskryf treffend die ongewone en kleurvolle lewe van hierdie man, een van die groot evangeliese predikers van die agtiende eeu. Sy getuienis was: “Deur die genade van God is ek wat ek is!”

“Amazing Grace” was ’n gesang wat in 1779 gepubliseer is, met woorde geskryf in 1772 deur die Engelse digter en Anglikaanse geestelike John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is waarskynlik die mees geliefde gesang van die afgelope twee eeue. Na raming word hierdie gesang jaarliks 10 miljoen keer uitgevoer. Dit het op meer as 11 000 albums verskyn en is in omtrent 60 tale vertaal. Dit is genoem in Harriet Beecher Stowe se anti-slawernyroman Uncle Tom’s Cabin. Dit het ’n oplewing in gewildheid gehad tydens twee van Amerika se grootste krisisse: die Burgeroorlog en die Viëtnam-oorlog.

Ironies genoeg is hierdie roerende lied, nou nou geassosieer met die Afro-Amerikaanse gemeenskap, geskryf deur ’n voormalige slawekoper, John Newton.

John is op 24 Julie 1725 in Wapping, Engeland, gebore, by ’n seeman-vader, John Newton Sr., en ’n vroom Christelike moeder, Elizabeth Newton. Sy vader het hom liefgehad maar was meestal op see weg. Sy moeder daarenteen was sag en koesterend en het hom die Woord van God geleer. Sy het hom geïndoktrineer om die Bybel hoofstukke op ’n slag te memoriseer en het hom na die kerk geneem. Ongelukkig is sy moeder, toe hy byna sewe was, aan tuberkulose oorlede. Sy vader het kort daarna weer getrou en hom na ’n kostskool gestuur. Tydens sy tyd by die kostskool het hy slegte vriende gekry. Sy karakter het so verval dat hy van een skool uitgesit en na ’n ander oorgeplaas is. Teen die tyd dat hy 11 jaar oud was, wou die kostskole hom nie hê nie, en sy vader het hom toe saamgeneem na see. Hy het die volgende ses jaar op die Atlantiese Oseaan saam met sy vader deurgebring.

Toe John 17 was, het sy vader gereël dat hy na Jamaika gestuur sou word vir ’n goedbetaalde pos om ’n plantasie te toesig. Op pad daarheen, terwyl hy gewag het vir die skip se vertrek, het John ’n uitnodiging gekry na die huis van ’n paar ou vriende, die Catletts. Dit was in hierdie huis dat John se moeder tien jaar vroeër gesterf het. Terwyl hy hul weer leer ken het, het hy hul dogter Mary ontmoet. John en Mary se moeder was die beste vriende. John was uitgenooi om vier dae te bly, maar hy het twee weke gebly en die skip na Jamaika gemis.

Op 18-jarige ouderdom is John in diens geneem deur die Koninklike Vloot, en sy lewe het van sleg na erger gegaan. Hy wou terugkeer en Mary sien, so hy het deserter en van die skip afgekom, maar is gevang, in die openbaar geslaan en in yster gelei. Sy lewe op die skip was so goddeloos dat selfs die ander goddelose seuns krimp in die aangesig van sy vloeke en laster. Hy het die bynaam “Die Groot Lasteraar” gekry en was so ongewenst op die skip dat hy na ’n slaweskip gestuur is om te werk.

Een van die eienaars van die slaweskip waar hy nou werk, het John ’n werk aangebied eens hulle die Afrikakus bereik het. Sodra hy egter aan wal was, is hy vasgebind en gedwing om te werk met min kos, klere of skuiling. Hy het gedurende hierdie tyd verskeie briewe aan sy vader gestuur en om hulp gesmeek.

’n Skip met die naam The Greyhound het naby die kus gesegel, wat John nou as sy tuiste beskou het. Die kaptein was deur John se vader opdrag gegee om na sy seun te soek. Die skip, al was hy amper te ver van die kus om handel te dryf, het besluit om tog handel te probeer. ’n Vriend van John het van die wal af uitgevaar om te ruil. Toe hy wegswaai, het die kaptein hom gevra of hy iemand met die naam John Newton geken. Tot die kaptein se verbasing het hy dit gedoen, en John is aan boord gebring om huis toe te gaan.

Aan boord van die skip het Newton ’n eksemplaar opgetel van Thomas á Kempis se Christen-klassikus The Imitation of Christ. Hy het nog nooit iets soortgelyks teëgekom nie, en hy het begin wonder of die Christelike aansprake dalk waar kon wees. Daardie nag, op 10 Maart 1748, het ’n woeste storm die skip byna laat sloer. Mans, diere en proviand is oorboord geslaan. Die storm het Newton ontwaak; die skip se rotte houtwerk is deur die golwe gebreek en vloedwater het in sy kajuit rondgespoel. John het vir die eerste keer in jare gebid.

The Greyhound het meer as 11 dae in die Noord-Atlantiese storm geslaan. Met min hoop op oorlewing het die matrose meganies aan die pompe gewerk om die vaartuig bo water te hou. Op die elfde dag van die storm was John te uitgeput om te pomp, en so is hy aan die roer vasgebind, waar hy sy beste gedoen het om die skip op koers te hou. Van een uur tot middernag was hy by die roer. Hy was bevrees hy sou sterf, en as die Christelike geloof waar was, sou hy sekerlik nie vergewe word nie. Hy het teruggedink oor alles wat hy oor die afgelope paar jaar gedoen het. Sy lewe het so verwoes en oorrompel gelyk soos die geskaafde skip wat hy probeer stuur deur die storm. Gedurende daardie lang en uitputtende ure het Newton tot God uitgeroep soos hy nog nooit tevore gedoen het nie, en dit was die keerpunt in sy lewe.

Daardie dag het John tot op die oor onthou. “Op daardie dag het die Here van bo af gestuur en my uit die diep waters geroei.” Meer as 50 jaar later het John in sy dagboek op 21 Maart 1805 geskryf: “Nie baie goed in staat om te skryf nie; maar ek probeer om die terugkeer van hierdie dag met vernedering, gebed en lofprysing te gedenk.”

Net God se wonderlike genade kon ’n onverskrokke, goddelose, slawebedrywende seeman neem en hom in ’n kind van God verander. John het nooit opgehou om in verwondering te staan oor God se werk in sy lewe nie. Hy het belangstelling ontwikkel in gebed, bybellees en -meditasie en om slegs woorde te praat wat God behaag.

Op sy terugkeer huis toe het Mary en haar ouers die verandering wat die Here in John gebring het, raakgesien. Die twee is op 1 Februarie 1750 in die huwelik bevestig.

Die volgende vier jaar was Newton kaptein van sy eie slaweskip. Hierdie beroep het hom maande lank van Mary geskei. Terwyl hulle van mekaar geskei was, het die twee voortdurend korrespondeer. In sy briewe het John herhaaldelik geskryf hoe hul liefde en huwelik sy dankbaarheid aan die Here verhoog het. “... Wanneer ek my verlustig in ’n besondere gedagte aan jou, dra dit my gewoonlik verder en bring my op my knieë om die Here te seën dat Hy so ’n skat aan my gegee het en om te bid vir jou vrede en welstand.”

John het gepoog om sy slaweskip te “Christianiseer” deur Sondagaanddienste vir sy bemanning van 30 sonde-geharde mans te hou. Hy het nog drie reise gemaak om slawe van Afrika na Noord-Amerika te bring. Terwyl hy sy vierde reis beplan het, het hy siek geword van malaria. God het hierdie siekte gebruik om sy betrokkenheid by die slawehandel te beëindig.

Toe John ’n nuwe hoofstuk in sy lewe begin het, het hy geroep gevoel om ’n predikant te wees. Vir meer as 50 jaar het hy die evangelie gepreek en was een van die invloedrykste mans van sy tyd.

John Newton het dikwels ’n gesang geskep vir sy Sondagaanddienste. In 1779 is 280 van hierdie gesange versamel en saam met 68 gesange deur Newton se vriend en parochiaan, William Cowper, gepubliseer as die Olney Hymns. Die bekendste van al die Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, het gegroei uit David se uitroep in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. Ons ken dit vandag as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” het oorspronklik ses stanza’s gehad, en die laaste vers is omtrent ’n eeu later bygevoeg. Die meeste liedeboeke bevat vier of vyf van hierdie verse.

As predikant in die kerk het John aanhoudend meer en meer beangs geraak oor die slawehandel wat steeds voortgegaan het. In 1788, 34 jaar nadat hy die slawehandel verlaat het, het hy ’n boek getiteld Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade geskryf en dit aan al die lede van die parlement gestuur. Hierdie boek het die publiek bewus gemaak van die euwels van die slawehandel. Hy haal dit aan: “Oorbodig om te sê, die vang, verkoop en vervoer van swart slawe na die plantasiëns in die Weste-Indië en Amerika was ’n wrede en bose manier van lewe.” Met die hulp en voorsienigheid van God het John die dag gesien, enkele maande voor sy dood in 1807, toe slawerny formeel in Engeland verban is.

Toe John in sy sestigs was, is sy geliefde vrou Mary oorlede. Dit was ’n groot beproewing vir John, en hy het die oorblywende 17 jaar van sy lewe sonder haar deurgebring.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

Die laaste woorde van John Newton terwyl hy op sy sterfbed gelê het, was soos volg: “Ek is nog in die land van die sterwendes; ek sal binnekort in die land van die lewendes wees.”

Die wysie “Amazing Grace” is ’n vroeë Amerikaanse volksmelodie. Dit was eerstens bekend as ’n plantasiemelodie met die titel “Loving Lambs”. Hierdie wysie is eers in 1831 gepubliseer in die boek The Virginia Harmony. Die meerderheid van die liedeboeke wat ná hierdie tyd gepubliseer is, het hierdie lied ingesluit. In 1910 het Edwin O. Excell die laaste vers bygevoeg, wat uiteindelik die laaste drie oorspronklike verse van die lied vervang het. Sy uitgawe van die lied is vandag die mees algemene in ons liedeboeke. Verskeie ander Olney hymns deur Newton word steeds vandag gesing, insluitend “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” en “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

Our Father’s world is a world unspoiled by human invention and intervention. While sin and technology have warped and stolen many lovely things from the human race, there abide still a few that remain unmarred by civilization. Little children in the fresh innocence of their unsoiled morning top the ranks as a bit of heaven on earth and call all observers heavenward. Another is the fowl of the air as prescribed in Genesis. Paul pleaded with the Corinthian church, “Doth not nature itself teach you?” We are exhorted to consider the lilies, the ravens, and the grass of the field. Each of these bears a significant dimension of the eternal God in their existence and gives us definition to their Creator. Perhaps all of nature can give us snapshots into heavenly places if we had the time and eyes to observe it.

Birds hold a unique place in God’s creation, for their sphere is in the heavens. Man may mount on the wings of a plane and evade the lower earth for a few hours, but the heavens will never be a place of his common dominion. The birds are a picture of a heavenly race, for they are at home there. They are a natural representation of the saints and angels of God and so we do well to give them due attention. While there may be dozens of lessons to be drawn from these vessels of grace and beauty, one of the most prominent and outstanding virtues will be observed in the song that they raise. Many animals dwelling on the earth are virtually mute. Of the ones that do speak, it is often to threaten or express complaint. “Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? Or loweth the ox over his fodder?” (Job 6:5). When they are happy and content, they have no message to convey. The dog barks at an intruder to drive him away, while the cat mews for attention. They speak when they are threatened or dissatisfied, in fear or in pain. Similarly, the earthly human shares its nature with the mammals of the field.

Birds are diverse. They exercise their joyous vocals so much that they are the epitome of happiness. The expression “happy as a lark” is so common a term that it is used by people who have never even ventured to the meadow to see or hear a lark. While some may inform us that these songs are mere mating calls and have little to do with their feelings, we cannot escape the inner conviction that, whether mating or not, these birds delight in bearing a jubilant expression of joy and we do well to let them teach us. “Is any merry? Let him sing psalms” (James 5:13). The birds do this incessantly and it seems impossible to draw any other conclusion but that they are happy while doing so. Wander near the nest of a swallow and you will find that they have ways of expressing depreciation as well. The killdeer also has no qualms with expressing rash disfavor to those who intrude their domain, but these are not to be mistaken as songs. The singing birds are a beautiful painted picture of the saints and angels of God.

How little knowledge of heaven is committed to our understanding. The scenes of heavens described and laid out before us in Revelations can hardly bring our finite minds into its infinite realm. One dimension that we can connect with is that it is a place filled with singing. Little wonder, for it is the culminating end of the contented and joy-filled saints of God, and there they will sing a new song. Nearly every scene at the throne in Revelations is marked by some dimension of praise. “And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God” (Ps 40:3). On 22 occasions, the Scriptures reiterate the phrase, I will sing.

It is the nature of the birds to sing. It is their waking thought as morning guilds the sky, and it flows from within them like a fountain. Not all of their songs are alike. Some are elaborate in their duration, meter, and pitch, while others are plain. Some merely chirp with a merry heart. The robin opens up the choir in early spring, but his song is soon surpassed in beauty by the song sparrow and again by the rose-breasted grosbeak. The song of the wren trumps them all for longevity and vibrancy. The canary sings in a cage, while the nightingale sings in the dark. The robins sing in the rain. The buntings fill in the heat of the day when other birds are silent. As diverse as their song may be, they all commonly burst forth in exuberant happiness. It is here that they shall instruct us.

“Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). The advent of Christ was marked by the angelic host announcing peace and goodwill toward men. All those who will bear His name must deliver the same tidings. In John 4, we happen upon the scene at Jacob’s well, where Christ asks the woman for a drink. Her reply seems to bear a tinge of bitterness. “Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.” Though she esteemed herself as a spiritual person and willingly followed Him into religious discourse, she had no song. Like the well that they speak over, her water was buried deep below the surface and how laborious the effort to bring it forth. Christ offers another alternative. “But the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:14).

The well of Christ is an artesian well. One needs neither pitcher nor labor to draw it out, for it spews forth abundantly on its own accord. While Christ is probably speaking of the Spirit as in John 7:38, surely this may be just as applicable to a joy-laden heart. What is a more apt outpouring to flow from a Christ-inspired wellspring than the rapture of a song? “Behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart” (Is 65:14). Now this should all seem plain enough to understand and easy enough to do but, alas, we find we have a constant and persistent adversary who seeks to thwart our song. We are not unaware of his devices...

Sin. Not all birds sing. There are some whose visage is black as sin. These only seem to screech and scream and are no example for the saints of God to emulate. The babbling noise we hear emanating from many passing vehicles certainly parallels the songs of such foul fowl. “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird” (Rev 18:2). These abundant creatures are the fallen spirits, the fowls waiting to devour the seed sown by the wayside. Of such are the worthless blackbirds, starlings, and grackles. The crows show themselves also at the roadside, feeding on rotting carcasses. Often you will find them in large numbers feeding themselves on the corn the farmer painstakingly planted for himself. So transgresses the selfish soul in his pursuit of happiness, feeding gleefully on the calamity of another and exploiting their sin. He bears no song, for his day is constantly clouded by the misdeeds of others who cross his path.

Neglect. The cowbird is also black (the female is brown/gray). She will be found sitting on a high vantage, shamelessly calling to her lovers by her shrill screeching. She then has the audacity to lay her egg in another bird’s nest, forcing them to raise her offspring. This is certainly a fitting emblem for a good number of females in our day. Though justified by circumstances, these women care not for their own, but are products of neglect. They have no lullaby to share with their young, for they have escorted them to the nest of another while her mind is preoccupied with work and business. “But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother’s breasts” (Ps 22:9). No doubt that the singing mother can implant copious songs in her infant and set the stage for a happy and hope-filled life. While we may show mercy to a woman in dire circumstances, the major song of modern women bears chords that are but dissident and melancholy. These are stopped-up wells like unto the wells that Isaac found upon his return to Gerar. The Philistines “had filled them with earth” (Gen 26:15). So run the spiritually neglected homes of many families today, who pack their schedules so full of earthly commitments that they have no time to spend an hour in song together. If the birds stopped singing, would they even notice?

Ingratitude. Find a soul bathed in unthankfulness, and you will find a soul without a song. If the canary were to refuse to sing in captivity, few of us would ever have heard his rollicking melody. “We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion. How shall we sing the LORD’S song in a strange land?” (Ps 137:2-4). God’s people had been instructed by Jeremiah to build houses, plant gardens, and raise families. “… And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer. 29:5-7). But they could see no worth in it. With their eyes fixed upon the dismal scene around them, they lost their song. Israel had within its history a rich tradition of song. Their singing erupted at the passage of the Red Sea in the days of Jehoshaphat and had been known to defeat armies. Earthly discomfort is no excuse to withhold gratitude, for our God reigns, and we are His children. Such were the conditions of the Philippian prison where two jailbirds, Paul and Silas, opened the concert at midnight and rocked the corridors with their joyful singing.

When we open our mouths and stretch our vocals in praise, we enact the grace of God. We join the faithful choir alongside Miriam, Deborah, and Hannah, and blend harmoniously with Moses, David, Paul, and Barnabas. At evening, we sing with our Lord and His disciples after supper, and with legions of angels “giving glory to God in the highest.” If that isn’t enough, perhaps we should consider rising at early dawn and singing with the innumerable hosts of our feathered friends who are thankful for God’s loving providence. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord … And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:16, 23).

Voëls het ’n unieke plek in God se skepping, want hul sfeer is in die hemele. Die mens mag op die vlerke van ’n vliegtuig klim en vir ’n paar ure die laer aarde ontvlug, maar die hemele sal nooit ’n plek van sy algemene heerskappy wees nie. Die voëls is ’n beeld van ’n hemelse ras, want hulle voel daar tuis. Hulle is ’n natuurlike voorstelling van die heiliges en engele van God en daarom doen ons goed om hulle behoorlik aandag te gee. Al mag daar dosyne lesse wees wat onttrek kan word uit hierdie vaatjies van genade en skoonheid, een van die mees prominente en uitstaande deugde sal in die lied waartoe hulle opstyg waargeneem word. Baie diere wat op die aarde woon is feitlik stom. Van diegene wat wel praat, is dit dikwels om te dreig of klagte te uiten. “Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? Or loweth the ox over his fodder?” (Job 6:5). Wanneer hulle gelukkig en tevrede is, het hulle geen boodskap om oor te dra nie. Die hond blaf vir ’n indringer om hom weg te jaag, terwyl die kat miaau vir aandag. Hulle praat wanneer hulle bedreig of ontevrede is, in vrees of in pyn. Net so deel die aardse mens sy natuur met die soogdiere van die veld.

Voëls is uiteenlopend. Hulle oefen hulle vreugdevolle vokale so gereeld uit dat hulle die personifiëring van geluk is. Die uitdrukking “happy as a lark” is so algemene ’n term dat dit deur mense gebruik word wat nog nooit eers na die weiding gegaan het om ’n leeu of ’n lark te sien of te hoor nie. Al mag sommige ons inlig dat hierdie liedere blote paringsroep is en min met hul gevoelens te doen het, kan ons nie ontsnap aan die innerlike oortuiging dat, paring of nie, hierdie voëls baie plesier vind daarin om ’n jubelende uitdrukking van vreugde te dra nie en ons doen goed om hulle te laat leer. “Is any merry? Let him sing psalms” (James 5:13). Die voëls doen dit onophoudelik en dit lyk onmoontlik om enige ander gevolgtrekking te trek as dat hulle gelukkig is terwyl hulle dit doen. Wandel naby die nes van ’n swael en jy sal vind dat hulle maniere het om ook verwerping uit te druk. Die killdeer het ook geen scrupules om onbesonne afkeer te betoon teenoor diegene wat hul gebied binnedring nie, maar dit moet nie verwar word met liedere nie. Die singvoëls is ’n pragtige geskilderde beeld van die heiliges en engele van God.

Hoe min kennis van die hemel is aan ons begrip toevertrou. Die tonele van die hemele wat in Revelations beskryf en voor ons uitgesprei word, kan skaars ons eindige verstand in sy oneindige ryk bring. Een dimensie waarmee ons kan skakel is dat dit ’n plek vol gesang is. Geen wonder nie, want dit is die kulminerende einde van die tevrede en vreugdevolle heiliges van God, en daar sal hulle ’n nuwe lied sing. Byna elke toneel by die troon in Revelations word gemerk deur ’n of ander dimensie van lof. “And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God” (Ps 40:3). Op 22 geleenthede herhaal die Skrif die frase, I will sing.

Dit is die natuur van die voëls om te sing. Dit is hulle wakkere gedagte wanneer die oggend die hemel vergul, en dit vloei uit hulle soos ’n fontein. Nie al hulle liedere is dieselfde nie. Sommige is ingewikkeld in hul duur, maat en toonhoogte, terwyl ander eenvoudig is. Sommige tjilp eenvoudig met ’n vrolike hart. Die robin open die koor vroeg in die lente, maar sy lied word gou oortref in skoonheid deur die song sparrow en weer deur die rose-breasted grosbeak. Die lied van die wren oorheers hulle almal in volharding en lewendigheid. Die kanarie sing in ’n hok, terwyl die nagingall sing in die donker. Die robins sing in die reën. Die buntings vul die hitte van die dag in wanneer ander voëls stil is. So uiteenlopend as hul lied ook mag wees, barst hulle almal gemeenlik uit in uitbundige blydskap. Hier sal hulle ons inlig.

“Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). Die koms van Christus is gemerk deur die engelike hemeltog wat vrede en welwil teenoor die mense aangekondig het. Al diegene wat sy naam sal dra, moet dieselfde boodskap oorbring. In John 4 tref ons die toneel by Jakobsput, waar Christus die vrou vir ’n slukkie water vra. Haar antwoord lyk na ’n toon van bitterheid. “Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.” Al het sy haarself as ’n geestelike persoon beskou en vrywillig saam met Hom in godsdienstige gesprek gegaan, het sy geen lied nie. Soos die put waaroor hulle praat, was haar water diep onder die oppervlak begrawe en hoe moeisaam die moeite om dit na vore te bring. Christus bied ’n ander alternatief. “But the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:14).

Die put van Christus is ’n artesiese put. Een het geen kruik of arbeid nodig om dit uit te trek nie, want dit spuit uit oorvloed op sy eie. Al praat Christus waarskynlik van die Gees soos in John 7:38, is dit seker net so toepaslik op ’n vreugde-gevulde hart. Wat is ’n meer geskikte uitstorting om uit ’n Christus-geïnspireerde bron te vloei as die vervoering van ’n lied? “Behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart” (Is 65:14). Nou behoort dit alles duidelik genoeg te wees om te verstaan en maklik genoeg om te doen, maar, helaas, ons vind dat ons ’n konstante en volhardende vyand het wat ons lied wil dwarsboom. Ons is nie ongebewus van sy toestelle nie...

Sonde. Nie alle voëls sing nie. Daar is sommige wie se voorkoms swart is soos sonde. Hierdie skyn net te skree en te gil en is geen voorbeeld vir die heiliges van God om na te boots nie. Die gepraat wat ons deur baie verbygaande voertuie hoor, loop beslis parallel met die liedere van sulke onreine voëls. “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit, and a cage of every unclean and hateful bird” (Rev 18:2). Hierdie oorvloedige wesens is die gevalle geeste, die voëls wat wag om die saad wat langs die pad gesaai is, te verslind. Van sulkes is die waardelose swartvoëls, starlings, en grackles. Die kraaie vertoon hulself ook by die padkant en voed op verrottende karkasse. Dikwels sal jy hulle in groot getalle vind wat hulleself voed aan die mielies wat die boer met moeite vir homself geplant het. So oorskry die selfsugtige siel in sy strewe na geluk, wat vrolik maal aan die ellende van ’n ander en hul sonde uitbuit. Hy dra geen lied nie, want sy dag is voortdurend bewaar met die verkeerde dade van ander wat sy pad kruis.

Verwaarlosing. Die koei-voël is ook swart (die wyfie is bruin/grys). Sy sal op ’n hoë uitkykpunt gesien word, skaamteloos haar minnaars lok met haar skril gekras. Sy het dan die brutale durf om haar eier in ’n ander voël se nes te lê en hulle te dwing om haar nageslag groot te maak. Dit is sekerlik ’n geskikte embleem vir ’n goeie aantal vroue in ons tyd. Al is hulle deur omstandighede geregverdig, gee hierdie vroue niks om vir hul eie nie, maar is produkte van verwaarlosing. Hulle het geen slaaplied om met hul kleintjies te deel nie, want hulle het hulle na ’n ander se nes gelei terwyl haar gedagtes besig is met werk en sake. “But thou art he that took me out of the womb: thou didst make me hope when I was upon my mother’s breasts” (Ps 22:9). Geen twyfel dat die singende moeder menige lied in haar baba kan ingeplant en die verhoog kan stel vir ’n gelukkige en hoopvolle lewe nie. Terwyl ons barmhartigheid kan wys aan ’n vrou in droewe omstandighede, dra die hooflied van moderne vroue akkorde wat maar dissonant en treurig is. Dit is toeslote putte soos die putte wat Isaac gevind het toe hy teruggekeer het na Gerar. Die Filistyne “had filled them with earth” (Gen 26:15). So hardloop die geestelik verwaarloosde huise van baie families vandag, wat hul skedules so vol pak met aardse verpligtinge dat hulle geen tyd het om ’n uur saam in gesang deur te bring nie. As die voëls ophou sing, sou hulle dit selfs opmerk?

Onvergenoegdheid. Vind ’n siel wat in ondankbaarheid bad, en jy sal ’n siel sonder ’n lied vind. As die kanarie sou weier om in gevangenskap te sing, sou min van ons ooit sy sprankelende melodie gehoor het. “We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion. How shall we sing the LORD’S song in a strange land?” (Ps 137:2-4). God se volk was deur Jeremiah geïnstrueer om huise te bou, tuine te plant en families groot te maak. “… And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer. 29:5-7). Maar hulle kon geen waarde daarin sien nie. Met hulle oë gefokus op die somber toneel om hulle, het hulle hul lied verloor. Israel het binne sy geskiedenis ’n ryk tradisie van gesang gehad. Hulle sang het opgespruit by die oorsteek van die Rooi See in die dae van Jehoshaphat en was bekend om leagues te verslaan. Aardse ongemak is geen verskoning om dankbaarheid te onthou nie, want ons God heers, en ons is Sy kinders. Só was die omstandighede in die Filippense tronk waar twee tronkvoëls, Paul en Silas, die konsert om middernag oopgemaak het en die gange geskud het met hul vreugdevolle gesang.

Wanneer ons ons monde oopmaak en ons vokale rek in lof, handel ons die genade van God uit. Ons sluit by die getroue koor aan langs Miriam, Deborah, en Hannah, en meng harmonies met Moses, David, Paul, en Barnabas. Saans sing ons met ons Here en Sy dissipels na ete, en met legioene engele “giving glory to God in the highest.” As dit nie genoeg is nie, behoort ons dalk te oorweeg om vroeg in die oggend op te staan en saam te sing met die ontelbare skare van ons veroetelde vriende wat dankbaar is vir God se liefdevolle voorsienigheid. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord … And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:16, 23).
